This lab has exercises that reinforce the section "Working on remote machines" of Lecture 4 (`lectures/lec04_remote_machines_postgres.qmd`) and the sections "Finding and stopping a process" and "Background job administration" of Lecture 2 (`lectures/lec02_linux_advanced.qmd`). Parts 1 and 2 get you onto Moriah, the HUJI cluster, and move files back and forth. In Parts 3 to 7 you run **everything on Moriah**. You will need a second terminal logged into Moriah in a few places.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Ground rules
* Run every command yourself. Many answers depend on what you see (and your PID numbers will not be the same as anyone else's).
* Leave the "#TODO text [question text] text" line and start a new line underneath and write your answers on that new line
* This file stays on your laptop, and you commit and push it from there. Keep it open on your laptop while your terminal is on Moriah.
* Moriah is **shared** and its login machine is used by everyone. Other people's programs will show up in your output, including your classmates' `sleep` commands from this very lab. Only ever touch your own processes. Run nothing heavy on the login machine: everything here just sleeps or prints a line per second.
* Clean up after yourself. Every part ends by stopping the processes it started. Check with `pgrep -u $USER -a sleep` that none are left over.
* **Never** put your private key (`~/.ssh/id_ed25519`) in this file or anywhere else.
:::

# Part 1: Remote computing with `ssh`

Log in to Moriah from your laptop, with your own login in place of the two `user` placeholders. Enter your OTP and your password.

```bash
ssh -J user@bava.cs.huji.ac.il user@moriah-gw.cs.huji.ac.il
#If you setup your machine using the instructions found in `04_setup_fast_ssh.qmd`, you will use simply the following instead
#and you will only need one OTP every four hours and no password (your keys are used in lieu).
ssh moriah
```

Now once inside the moriah gateway computer, run the following:

```bash
hostname
whoami
cd ~
pwd
nproc
free -h
exit #go back to your laptop
```

Now run the same `hostname`, `pwd`, `nproc` and `free -h` on your laptop (a Mac has no `free`: use `sysctl -n hw.memsize`, which is in bytes).

#TODO [Why is the `pwd` different on Moriah vs your laptop? <1pts>]
pwd shows the current directory. I ran it from my home directory on each machine. On my Mac, that directory is /Users/mkhlaily76. On Moriah, it is /sci/home/muhammad.khala.

moriah-gw is on the university’s internal network. From home, I connect through bava, a jump host that forwards my SSH connection to Moriah.

# Part 2: Moving files with `rsync`

All of these commands are run **on your laptop**, in `labs/04/scratch`. First make a folder on the server, without logging in:

```bash
cd $my_52002_repo/labs/04/scratch
#TODO [login to moriah and make the folder lab04 in your home directory <1pts>]
mkdir -p ~/lab04
```

Send the data over and check that it arrived whole. `md5sum` prints a *checksum*, a short code computed from all of the bytes of a file (we will dicussing this more formally when we do hash functions), so two equal codes mean two equal files (on a Mac, use `md5 covid.csv` for the first line):

```bash
md5sum covid.csv
time #TODO [the rsync command which copies covid.csv to the lab04 folder on Moriah <1pts>]
time rsync -av -e 'ssh -J muhammad.khala@bava.cs.huji.ac.il' \
  covid.csv 'muhammad.khala@moriah-gw.cs.huji.ac.il:~/lab04/'
#TODO [login to moriah and run "md5sum ~/lab04/covid.csv" <1pts>]
md5sum ~/lab04/covid.csv
# a632887edbaaac09a20cfa9745c03b03  /sci/home/muhammad.khala/lab04/covid.csv

```

#TODO [how long did the `rsync` transfer take, and do the two checksums agree? <1pts>]
The rsync command took 26.071 seconds, including SSH authentication. The MD5 checksums on my Mac and on Moriah matched.

Make a folder of many small files, one per day, the same way you did in Lab 2:

```bash
mkdir days
awk -F, 'NR>1 {print > ("days/" $1 ".csv")}' covid.csv
ls days | wc -l
```

Copy the entire folder with `rsync`, twice:

```bash
time rsync -a --stats days/ moriah:~/lab04/days_rsync/
time rsync -a --stats days/ moriah:~/lab04/days_rsync/
```

#TODO [Why was the second `rsync` run so much faster? <2pts>]
The second run was faster because the files on Moriah already matched the local files in size and modification time. rsync sent the file list and protocol information and transferred 0 files. The total time, including SSH authentication, went from 33.225 seconds to 27.009 seconds.
#TODO [the `--stats` output has a line "Total bytes sent". What was it in each of the two rsync runs? <1pts>]
First run: 35,905,249 bytes sent. Second run: 13,574 bytes sent. My version of rsync labels this field Total sent.

Clean up on both sides:

```bash
rm -r days 
# TODO [login to moriah and cleanup covid.csv and the days/ folder <2pts>]
rm ~/lab04/covid.csv
/bin/rm -r -- "$HOME/lab04/days_rsync"
```

# Part 3: Looking at processes with `ps` and `pgrep`

From here to the end of the lab, everything is done on Moriah (unless it says otherwise):

```bash
#TODO [login to moriah <0pts>]
cd ~/lab04
```

`sleep 600` does nothing for 10 minutes, which makes it a perfect process to look at. The `&` at the end runs it in the **background**, so you get your prompt back. The shell stores the PID of the last background process in the variable `$!`:

```bash
sleep 600 &
echo $!
```

#TODO [what did the line `[1] <number>` that appeared after the first command show, and how is `echo $!` related to it? <1pts>]
`[1]` is the job number in my shell, and `1383726` is the process ID (PID). `echo $!` printed the PID of the last process I started in the background.

```bash
jobs
```

#TODO [Is the output of the above expected? Why/why not? <1pts>]
Yes. jobs showed sleep 600 as job [1] with status running, because I started it in the background with & and it was still running.

Now let's find this job in the linux process list. `ps` can show just the columns you ask for, for just the processes you ask for. Read the `-o` and `-p` options in `man ps` and run:

```bash
ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,command -p $!
#TODO [the parent PID of your `sleep` is the PID of another process. Write the command that shows that process' command, and say what it is <1pts>]
ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,command -p 1321977
# The parent process was my login shell, -zsh (PID 1321977).
```

```bash
#TODO [keep following the parents upward, one `ps` at a time, until you find the program which let you into moriah. The user will be "root". <1pts>]
ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,command -p 1321971
ps -ww -o pid,ppid,user,stat,command -p 1321694
# sleep (1383726) was started by zsh (1321977).
# zsh was started by sshd-session (1321971).
# Its parent was the privileged sshd-session (1321694), owned by root.
```

#TODO [How does this explain why your background job is at risk when the connection drops? <1pts>]
sleep was started by the shell in my SSH session. If the connection drops, the shell may exit and send a SIGHUP signal to the background job, which can stop it.

```bash
#TODO [How many different users (besides root) on Moriah have a `sleep` running right now? <2pts>]
ps -C sleep -o user:32= | awk 'NF && $1 != "root" {print $1}' | sort -u | wc -l
# Result: 2 users, excluding root.
```

#TODO [Print out a table of the users running sleep. <2pts>]
COUNT USER
    1 orzuk
    2 root
    1 shmuelhart

```bash
#TODO [kill your sleep job without losing your connection to moriah <1pts>]
sleep 600 &
sleep_pid=$!
kill "$sleep_pid"

```

# Part 4: A terminal that survives: `tmux`

`tmux` keeps a whole **terminal** alive, so that you can go away and come back to see it as you left it. Start a session called `lab4` on Moriah (if you get `command not found`, look for it with `module spider tmux`, as in the lecture):

```bash
tmux new -s lab4
```

You are now inside tmux (note the green bar at the bottom). We now navigate to the shared folder where there's a program you should run that persists.

```bash
cd /sci/courses/2026/52002/shared/
```

Now run the shared program called `tmux_proof`. Run it with your name as follows.

```bash
./tmux_proof "<first name> <last name>" #fill in your first name and last name!
```

After 24hr it will print out a unique encrypted code. We will decode it to reveal your full name and the hostname of the computer (which should be moriah). So don't share codes as you won't get credit if your name doesn't appear.

Detach: press Ctrl+B, release both keys, then press d. You are back in your normal terminal on Moriah. Then go back into the terminal and ensure it's still running.

```bash
tmux ls
tmux attach -t lab4
```
Detach again: press Ctrl+B, release both keys, then press d.

Now you can skip the next TODO and continue the rest of the assignment. You can exit moriah and come back in 24hr and it will still be running.


```bash
tmux ls
tmux attach -t lab4
#now copy the code
```

#TODO [write the encrypted code from tmux_proof after it completes <2pts>]

After the code is pasted above, you should cleanup your `tmux` terminal:

```bash
tmux kill-session -t lab4
tmux ls #ensures it's not there
exit #leave moriah and return to your own computer
```

Now make a common mistake on purpose: run your `\copy` line a second time.

```sql

```

#TODO [What happened, and why did postgres not stop you? <1pts>]
The second \copy appended the same rows again, doubling the row count. PostgreSQL allowed the duplicate rows because the table had no primary key or unique constraint.

```sql

```

#TODO [Look at the deaths column of your answer above. What went wrong? Write the corrected query below, using a condition from the lecture <2pts>]
PostgreSQL sorts NULL values first by default when using ORDER BY deaths DESC. The first query therefore returned rows with missing death counts. Adding deaths IS NOT NULL excludes those rows before ranking the counties.

```sql
#TODO [corrected query <1pts>]
SELECT county, state, deaths
FROM covid
WHERE date = '2020-11-30'
  AND deaths IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY deaths DESC
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10;

-- Bergen       | New Jersey   | 2124
-- Suffolk      | New York     | 2053
-- Hidalgo      | Texas        | 2050
-- Philadelphia | Pennsylvania | 2026
-- Clark        | Nevada       | 1767
#TODO [on 2020-12-31, the state, county and deaths of every county in Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont (write the states as a list, not with OR), sorted by state and, within each state, by deaths, most first <1pts>]
SELECT state, county, deaths
FROM covid
WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
  AND state IN ('Maine', 'New Hampshire', 'Vermont')
ORDER BY state ASC, deaths DESC;

-- First five rows:
-- Maine | Cumberland   | 97
-- Maine | York         | 63
-- Maine | Androscoggin | 44
-- Maine | Kennebec     | 29
-- Maine | Somerset     | 21

SELECT county, state, cases, deaths

WHERE date = '2020-12-31'

  AND cases < 200

#TODO [the number of different county names that contain "lake", first with LIKE and then with ILIKE <1pts>]
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT county) AS like_count
FROM covid
WHERE county LIKE '%lake%';
-- Result: 0

FROM covid

-- Result: 7
```

#TODO [Why do the two counts differ? <1pts>]
LIKE is case-sensitive, so %lake% matched 0 distinct county names. ILIKE is case-insensitive, so it also matched names containing Lake with a capital L. It returned 7 distinct names.

```sql
#TODO [for Florida on 2020-12-31 (one row per county), in one query with no GROUP BY: the total, mean (rounded), smallest, largest, standard deviation (rounded) and median of the counties' deaths <2pts>]
SELECT SUM(deaths) AS total_deaths,
       ROUND(AVG(deaths)) AS mean_deaths,
       MIN(deaths) AS min_deaths,
       MAX(deaths) AS max_deaths,
       ROUND(STDDEV(deaths)) AS sd_deaths,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY deaths) AS median_deaths
FROM covid
WHERE state = 'Florida'
  AND date = '2020-12-31';

FROM covid
WHERE date = '2020-12-31';

-- Result: 0
```

## Grouped aggregate queries

```sql
#TODO [on 2020-12-31, the total deaths of each state, with the column named total_deaths; show the 5 states with the fewest <1pts>]
SELECT state, SUM(deaths) AS total_deaths
FROM covid
WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY total_deaths ASC, state ASC
LIMIT 5;

-- Northern Mariana Islands | 2
-- Virgin Islands           | 23
-- Guam                     | 123
-- Vermont                  | 136
-- Alaska                   | 198

SELECT state, COUNT(DISTINCT county) AS n_counties
FROM covid
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY n_counties ASC, state ASC
LIMIT 3;

-- District of Columbia     | 1
-- Guam                     | 1
-- Northern Mariana Islands | 3
#TODO [the total cases in the whole country on each day of the first week of April 2020 (April 1 to 7), oldest first <1pts>]
SELECT date, SUM(cases) AS total_cases
FROM covid
WHERE date BETWEEN '2020-04-01' AND '2020-04-07'
GROUP BY date
ORDER BY date ASC;

-- 2020-04-01 | 215391
-- 2020-04-02 | 245108
-- 2020-04-03 | 277426
-- 2020-04-04 | 312525
-- 2020-04-05 | 338141
-- 2020-04-06 | 369057
-- 2020-04-07 | 399394
#TODO [for each state on 2020-12-31, in one query: the number of counties, the mean of cases (rounded) and the median of cases, named n_counties, mean_cases and median_cases; show the 3 states with the highest mean <2pts>]
SELECT state,
       COUNT(DISTINCT county) AS n_counties,
       ROUND(AVG(cases)) AS mean_cases,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY cases) AS median_cases
FROM covid
WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY AVG(cases) DESC, state ASC
LIMIT 3;

-- California           | 58 | 39791 | 8493.5
-- Arizona              | 15 | 34922 | 11126
-- District of Columbia |  1 | 28983 | 28983
#TODO [for each state, the first date it reported a death, with the column named first_death; show the 5 earliest <2pts>]
SELECT state, MIN(date) AS first_death
FROM covid
WHERE deaths > 0
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY first_death ASC, state ASC
LIMIT 5;

-- Washington   | 2020-02-29
-- California   | 2020-03-04
-- Florida      | 2020-03-06
-- New Jersey   | 2020-03-10
-- South Dakota | 2020-03-10
```
